summaries.example: Imagine you notice that a classmate is left out of a game. You could keep playing, or you could invite them in. Leibniz would say that wise goodness means understanding why kindness helps another person and then acting to help. The good choice is not only about getting a reward. It is also about caring for the other person’s happiness.
summaries.summary: Leibniz’s ethics asks what makes life good and how people should act. He describes three connected kinds of good. Metaphysical good is reality and order. Moral good is virtue, or a well-trained ability to act wisely. Physical good is pleasure. Leibniz thinks these fit together: understanding the order and beauty of the world can lead us to care about other people and act well. He presents justice as wise love for others. His natural-law view says that moral rules are not made right merely because God chooses them; instead, justice rests on lasting truths. Leibniz also says that people are moved by desires, some noticed clearly and some felt only vaguely. Reason, education, and good habits can help us manage these desires. He believes true happiness is lasting pleasure connected with knowledge and virtue. His writings also raise a question about progress: can the world and its minds become more perfect over time, or does the total amount of perfection stay the same? Finally, he criticizes Descartes and Stoic-style ethics for offering patience in difficult circumstances without enough hope that the world is wisely ordered and that justice will finally be done.
key_ideas: Leibniz connected goodness with order, virtue, and pleasure.
He thought people should try to imitate God’s wisdom and universal care as far as humans can.
Knowledge should guide action; simply thinking about what is good is not enough.
He believed that preparing good habits can help people make better choices when they feel tempted.
He saw justice as caring wisely about the good of others.
Leibniz thought happiness grows through learning, virtue, and lasting understanding, not just through short-lived pleasures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz gives a picture of ethics in which thinking, feeling, and acting belong together. His view encourages people to learn, build good habits, care about others, and consider long-term happiness instead of chasing every quick reward. It also invites an important question: should moral rules depend on someone’s command, or can reason show why fairness and kindness matter?

important_terms.definition: A quality of something that makes it more complete, ordered, or excellent. Leibniz thought perfection comes in degrees.
A good habit of acting with wisdom. Leibniz especially valued caring about the happiness of others.
A kind of love that takes joy in another person’s well-being, rather than helping only to get something back.
A set of moral rules that Leibniz believed people can understand through reason, such as rules against harming others.

questions_to_think_about: Can a person help someone else because they truly care and still feel happy about helping?
Why might learning more help someone make kinder choices?
Is it enough to know what is right, or must we also practice doing it?
Which is more lasting: a quick pleasure or the joy of understanding something important?

summaries.example: Suppose a student discovers that a popular snack contains a substance that may harm a classmate with an allergy. Immediate appetite favors eating it, while practical reason recognizes a more important good: protecting another person and preserving the group’s well-being. For Leibniz, a virtuous response requires more than knowing this fact. The student must attend to it, resist a misleading pleasure, and act from a stable concern for the other person’s good. The resulting satisfaction is not merely a reward added from outside; it is pleasure in a rationally understood good.
summaries.summary: Leibniz’s ethics is woven into his theology and metaphysics rather than presented in one independent ethical treatise. Its central directive is to imitate divine perfection as far as human beings can. His theory of the good is composite. Metaphysical good is reality, understood as limited degrees of perfection and harmony; moral good is virtue; physical good is pleasure. Pleasure is a perception of perfection, while pain is a perception of imperfection. Yet Leibniz is not simply a hedonist: lasting happiness depends on knowledge of order, God, the world, and other minds, together with active efforts to promote rational order and the welfare of others. Justice is the highest virtue because it is wise love, or benevolence guided by understanding. His natural-law theory holds that universal moral requirements are grounded in eternal rational truths, not in an arbitrary divine decision. He organizes justice into strict right, equity, and piety, moving from avoiding harm to giving others their due and finally to a comprehensive concern shaped by divine governance and the soul’s immortality. In moral psychology, desires motivate all action, but their objects differ. A person can act from an inclination whose satisfaction brings pleasure while desiring another person’s happiness for its own sake. Ignorance, error, and failures of attention explain much wrongdoing; education, deliberation, and advance commitments can strengthen the will. Leibniz also considers whether perfection increases through history and criticizes Cartesian ethics for offering endurance without the hope supplied by divine wisdom, providence, and justice.
key_ideas: Leibniz combines Platonic, perfectionist, and hedonist elements: reality or harmony, virtue, and pleasure are different but related goods.
Knowledge of order and perfection is necessary for happiness, but moral goodness also requires actively promoting order and the good of others.
Justice has degrees: strict right forbids harm, equity gives others their due and promotes their welfare, and piety extends justice across the whole course of existence.
Leibniz argues against voluntarism: moral standards do not become valid simply because God wills them, just as mathematical truths do not depend on a decree.
His moral psychology reconciles psychological egoism with altruism by distinguishing the pleasure that satisfies a desire from the object the desire is about.
Leibniz’s writings leave a debated question about progress: the world may develop toward greater perfection, but other passages suggest that total perfection remains constant.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz’s position connects moral philosophy with questions about reality, knowledge, motivation, religion, and the future. It challenges a sharp opposition between self-interest and concern for others: one’s happiness can depend on loving another’s good without reducing that good to a tool. It also shows how assumptions about God’s nature and the afterlife can shape theories of justice, hope, responsibility, and moral progress.

important_terms.definition: The view that goodness is connected with reality or being. Since created things have limited reality, they also have limited perfection.
Leibniz’s view that the good life involves developing the powers and capacities that belong to human nature, especially reason and benevolence.
Leibniz’s account of justice as wise love directed toward the happiness and perfection of others.
Universal moral principles that Leibniz holds to be independent of God’s arbitrary choice and knowable through reason.
The position that moral obligation depends on a free command or decision of God. Leibniz rejects this form of voluntarism.
A conscious desire or choice. Leibniz contrasts volitions with less clearly noticed desires called appetitions.
A desire or tendency that may operate below clear awareness and still incline a person toward action.
Love directed toward another’s happiness or perfection for its own sake, even though enjoying that happiness also gives the lover pleasure.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that a virtuous action satisfies the agent’s inclination make it selfish, or can the object of the desire remain another person’s good?
Why does Leibniz think that moral standards would become arbitrary if they depended only on divine choice?
Are knowledge and correct action jointly sufficient for happiness in Leibniz’s system? What role do habit and attention play?
Can a world be the best possible world while its inhabitants continue to improve?
Does Leibniz’s criticism of Cartesian ethics depend mainly on different views about God, the soul, or moral responsibility?

summaries.example: Suppose your friends want to spread a rumor because it is exciting. You know it may embarrass someone, but you also feel pressure to join in. Leibniz would say that a better choice involves more than obeying a rule. You should understand the harm, remember that the other person’s happiness matters, and use a habit of careful thinking to resist the excitement. If you help stop the rumor, your satisfaction can come from the person’s well-being, not just from avoiding punishment.
summaries.summary: Leibniz’s ethical theory is part of a larger system about God, reality, knowledge, and human action. He describes three connected kinds of good. Metaphysical good is reality and harmony; moral good is virtue; physical good is pleasure. Perfection is not all-or-nothing: created things have different, limited degrees of it. Leibniz thinks knowledge of order and beauty can produce wise love for others. Justice is therefore more than obeying rules. It involves avoiding harm, giving people their due, and widening one’s concern for their happiness. He calls these levels strict right, equity, and piety. Leibniz also says that moral laws are natural laws: they are grounded in reason and eternal truths, rather than being made right only by God’s free decision. This separates him from voluntarist thinkers. His account of motivation is complex. All actions arise from desires, including desires we do not clearly notice. But desires can have different objects. Someone may desire another person’s happiness for its own sake, while still receiving pleasure when that happiness occurs. Thus Leibniz tries to bring together self-interest and concern for others. He explains weakness of will partly as a failure to keep important knowledge in mind, so education, habits, and advance plans can improve action. He also asks whether the best possible world allows moral progress. Some of his writings suggest continuing development, while others suggest that the world’s total perfection stays constant. His criticism of Descartes focuses on whether a person can have hope in divine wisdom, purpose, and final justice.
key_ideas: Leibniz separates good into metaphysical, moral, and physical forms: reality and harmony, virtue, and pleasure.
He thinks knowledge helps create virtue, but people must also act to increase order and happiness.
Natural law is based on reason and eternal truths, not merely on God’s changing choice.
Justice has levels: do not harm people, give people what they are owed, and live with a wider concern for everyone’s good.
People act from desires, but desires can focus on different objects. Wanting another person’s happiness can be genuine even if helping also makes us happy.
Leibniz is uncertain, and later interpreters disagree, about whether the universe as a whole becomes more perfect over time.
summaries.why_it_matters: This philosophy helps us examine familiar questions in a more careful way. Is morality based on commands, reasons, or both? Can caring about others also contribute to our own happiness? Does knowing the right thing make us do it? Leibniz’s answers connect daily choices with broad questions about justice, knowledge, responsibility, hope, and human improvement.

important_terms.definition: The degree to which something is real, ordered, and complete. Leibniz says created things have limited perfection, while God has infinite perfection.
A trained tendency to act wisely and well. Leibniz treats justice as the most important virtue.
A moral rule that people can discover through reason and that does not depend simply on a ruler’s command.
Justice understood as wise care for the happiness and improvement of other people.
A theory saying that moral rules are right only because God freely chooses or commands them. Leibniz argues against it.
A desire that is clearly noticed, such as a deliberate wish to choose one action.
A partly hidden desire or pull that can influence action even when we do not clearly notice it.
Taking pleasure in another person’s happiness or excellence as the thing you care about, rather than helping only for a separate reward.

questions_to_think_about: If helping someone makes you feel good, does that cancel the kindness of your action?
Why might a rule be less trustworthy if it were right only because a powerful being happened to choose it?
How can planning ahead help someone resist a temptation later?
Can learning more about the world make someone morally better? Why might knowledge alone not be enough?
What would count as progress in a person: more knowledge, more happiness, more virtue, or all three?
